newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: INTERVIEW-Sparks sees big farm growth in E. Europe.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Sparks sees big farm growth in E. Europe.

text.p: Eastern Europe's shabby farm economies have the capacity to double or triple their current output but will need many years of high commodity prices to fund investment, a top agricultural consultant said Tuesday.

U.S. consultant Willard Sparks told Reuters in an interview that the potential of Eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union is as enormous as its challenges, and the region will weigh ever more heavily on world commodity markets.

"Basically it tells us that the world is not going to run out of food any time soon," said Sparks, head of Sparks Companies of Memphis, Tenn. But he added "It may be 10 or 15 years before Eastern Europe finds its potential."
He said, "The land is there and the productivity is there but we have no management, we have no technology and we have no irrigation, so it's going to take high prices."

Eastern European farmland is similar to that in Western Europe, and eastern farm output should eventually follow a similar path to the big growth in the west in recent decades, Sparks said. He singled out Poland as a country which might develop its farm output fairly quickly if it gains speedy entry to the European Union.
But agricultural growth might come more quickly in Latin America, which is way ahead of most of Eastern Europe in the liberalization and modernization of its economies.
"I think the first thing you're going to see is more grassland ploughed up in Argentina before you are going to see major increases in Eastern Europe," Sparks said.
While sown area in Argentina has expanded in recent years, it could gain much new cropland by pushing its beef herds into dryer lands.

"Argentina is one of the few places that has a lot of grassland that can easily be turned to crops. In the U.S. we did all that in the 60s and 50s," Sparks said, "Argentina still has cattle and grains mixed together, and it seems to me that the grains get so high that we have to plough up more of that grassland over the next five to 10 years."
Argentina could do this without much effect on its beef production, if it improved its efficiency to levels similar to those in the United States, Sparks said.
The Argentine government expects grain output to have soared in 1996/97 to about 56 million tonnes, easily beating the previous record of 46 million tonnes in 1995/96.
